Today it's her skills in business which have expanded the label to some 30 stores worldwide, from New York to Beijing. CNN's Andrew Stevens caught up with the designer in Hong Kong to talk about what it's like to lead both the business and creative direction of a global fashion line. Tam: The business side is like designing, it's like I like the touch of the fabric, I like to know the details about it. And you feel about it, you know about the deal, because who's the person who knows what the best deal for you is? Yourself. It's like designing clothes, I love to know how to solve every single thing, you know. Like what kind of budget . Stevens: It's just natural curiosity? Tam: Natural curiosity, I love it. I love every aspect of it. Stevens: Who have you learned your business skills from or have you made it up as you went along? Tam: I self-taught myself in business; I know nothing about the business, I learned everything -- about the pricing, the shipping, the contracts, everything -- by doing it. When you're doing it yourself, you know everything. If you don't do it, you just listen to somebody telling you how to do it, you're not experiencing it. Once you're experiencing it, you can grow so much from it. Once you experience it, you can go further, much further. It's a feeling of it. Stevens: When you won the Hong Kong businesswoman of the year award, you said that your mother was one of your greatest inspirations. How did she inspire you? Tam: She inspired me so much you know, like you say, the determination, persistence. When she really wanted to make something, she would really go to the end, she'd really want to make it happen and I see her, she's really the force behind me. We were quite poor, we had no money, my parents were working really hard. When I grew up, I saw them working so hard, and then deep inside myself that I wanted to change the situation, I wanted to make something, this one thing. Stevens: What do you think are the most important qualities for a businessperson? Tam: For me, it's most important, a vision, determination, and to never say no to yourself. And be open to criticisms, open to learning, and open to criticisms and knowing nothing about the business; nothing, so you can learn everything by knowing nothing, you know, and be successful in the things that you didn't know. Stevens: You work in a very creative industry, how do you keep your staff motivated in this industry, how do you keep them going, how do you keep them working for you? Tam: I always tell them my story, how I was in school when my teacher asked for one outfit -- I give them 8 outfits. I told them, do things that I didn't ask you, give me, do your work with passion, it's more important than "Oh, 6 o'clock, I have to leave." Do something that is out of the box. E-mail to a friend .

***

**HONG KONG, China (CNN)** — From the runway to the retail floor, Vivienne Tam seamlessly bridges the gap between artistic creativity and sharp business acumen. The renowned designer recently sat down with CNN’s Andrew Stevens on *The Boardroom* to discuss her remarkable journey. 

Since entering the fashion industry in the early 1980s and establishing her namesake brand in the 1990s, Tam has achieved international acclaim for her signature East-meets-West aesthetic. Today, her commercial strategy has expanded the label to approximately 30 stores worldwide, spanning from New York to Beijing. CNN caught up with Tam in Hong Kong to explore what it takes to steer both the creative vision and business direction of a global fashion brand.

***

**Andrew Stevens:** How do you balance the artistic and commercial sides of the brand?

**Vivienne Tam:** To me, managing the business is very much like designing. Just as I want to feel the texture of a fabric, I want to understand every detail of our operations. You need an intuitive feel for a deal because no one understands what is best for your business better than you do. Like crafting a collection, I enjoy solving every challenge—including the financials and budgeting.

**Stevens:** Is that driven by natural curiosity?

**Tam:** It is natural curiosity. I genuinely love every aspect of what I do.

**Stevens:** From whom did you learn your business acumen, or did you learn as you went along?

**Tam:** I am entirely self-taught. I started with no formal business training and learned every facet of the operation—from pricing and shipping to negotiating contracts—through hands-on experience. When you manage these details yourself, you gain a true mastery of the business. Listening to advice is one thing, but firsthand experience is irreplaceable; it drives profound growth and enables you to push your boundaries much further.

**Stevens:** When you were named Hong Kong Businesswoman of the Year, you cited your mother as one of your greatest inspirations. How did she influence you?

**Tam:** She inspired me immensely, particularly through her determination and persistence. Whenever she set her mind to something, she pursued it relentlessly until it was accomplished—she was truly the force behind me. We grew up in modest circumstances, and watching my parents work so hard instilled a deep inner drive within me to transform our situation and achieve something meaningful.

**Stevens:** What do you consider the most vital qualities for a business professional?

**Tam:** Above all: vision, determination, and a refusal to self-impose limits. It is equally important to remain receptive to criticism and continuous learning. Entering an industry without prior knowledge can actually be an advantage; it allows you to learn with an open mind and ultimately succeed in unfamiliar territory.

**Stevens:** In such a fast-paced creative field, how do you keep your staff motivated and dedicated?

**Tam:** I often share a story from my student days: when a teacher assigned a single outfit, I delivered eight. I encourage my team to go beyond what is asked of them and to approach their work with genuine passion, rather than simply watching the clock until 6:00 PM. I push them to think outside the box.

***

**Hong Kong: Where Global Dynamism Meets the Heart of China**

Situated on the vibrant southeastern coast of **China**, **Hong Kong** stands as one of the world’s most dynamic and captivating metropolises. Renowned for its iconic skyline, deep natural harbor, and relentless energy, this international financial hub represents a fascinating intersection of history, culture, and economic innovation.

For over a century, **Hong Kong** developed under British administration, evolving from a modest group of fishing villages into a booming global trading port. A historic turning point occurred in 1997, when sovereignty was handed back to **China**. Under the "One Country, Two Systems" framework, **Hong Kong** maintained its distinct legal system, capitalist economy, and unique way of life. Today, it serves as a critical bridge between mainland **China** and the rest of the world, facilitating trade, finance, and international diplomacy.

Standing along Victoria Harbour, visitors are treated to a breathtaking architectural spectacle. Dense clusters of modern glass-and-steel skyscrapers rise sharply against a backdrop of lush, emerald mountains. As an economic powerhouse, **Hong Kong** boasts one of the world's busiest ports and major financial exchanges, playing an essential role in the ongoing economic story of **China** and the broader Asia-Pacific region.

Beyond its financial prestige, **Hong Kong** is a cultural melting pot where East truly meets West. Traditional Cantonese customs remain deeply woven into the fabric of daily life. Centuries-old Taoist temples nestle between soaring commercial towers, traditional *feng shui* principles guide modern construction, and neon-lit street markets coexist with high-end luxury boutiques. The city is also a global culinary capital, famous for everything from traditional dim sum served in bustling teahouses to street-side *dai pai dongs* and Michelin-starred dining.

While often pictured as a densely populated concrete jungle, over 40 percent of **Hong Kong** consists of protected country parks and nature reserves. Just a short journey from the bustling city center lies a tranquil landscape of scenic hiking routes—such as the famous Dragon’s Back—white-sand beaches, and dozens of serene offshore islands in the South **China** Sea.

As **Hong Kong** continues to adapt and integrate into the dynamic Greater Bay Area initiative alongside mainland **China**, it retains its unique charm and identity. It remains a city of boundless vitality—a place where history, global enterprise, and deep-rooted traditions continuously shape a remarkable story.

Here is a transcript based on CNN’s *The Boardroom* featuring host Andrew Stevens in conversation with fashion designer Vivienne Tam. 

***

**PROGRAM:** CNN International – *The Boardroom*  
**HOST:** Andrew Stevens  
**GUEST:** Vivienne Tam (Fashion Designer & Founder, Vivienne Tam)

---

### **[GRAPHIC: CNN THE BOARDROOM]**

**ANDREW STEVENS (VOICEOVER):**  
It is a brand defined by a seamless blend of East and West. Long before China became the powerhouse of the global luxury market, one designer was already taking traditional Chinese motifs, culture, and craftsmanship, and translating them for the world’s most glamorous runways. 

Born in Guangzhou, raised in Hong Kong, and forged in the competitive fashion capital of New York, Vivienne Tam built a global empire by proving that "Made in China" could mean high fashion, high quality, and high art.

Welcome to *The Boardroom*. I’m Andrew Stevens. Today, we sit down with fashion pioneer Vivienne Tam to talk about building a global brand, changing Western perceptions of Asian design, and navigating the rapidly shifting landscape of modern fashion.

---

### **[SCENE START: INTERVIEW SET – URBAN STUDIO OVERLOOKING THE HONG KONG SKYLINE]**

**ANDREW STEVENS:**  
Vivienne, thank you so much for joining us on *The Boardroom*.

**VIVIENNE TAM:**  
Thank you for having me, Andrew. It’s a pleasure to be here.

**ANDREW STEVENS:**  
When you first moved to New York in the 1980s with a bag full of your designs, the fashion industry was very different. Western aesthetics dominated, and "Made in China" was often associated with cheap mass production, not couture. What was it like trying to break through those barriers back then?

**VIVIENNE TAM:**  
It was extremely challenging. When I first brought my collection to buyers in New York, many people didn't understand what I was trying to do. They looked at Asian motifs—like dragons, Buddha images, traditional embroidery—and they thought of costume, or something you’d find in a souvenir shop. They didn't see it as modern fashion. 

I had to convince them that Eastern culture could be contemporary, chic, and universally appealing. I called it "East-meets-West," but to me, it was simply about bringing my heritage into the modern world.

**ANDREW STEVENS:**  
Was there a specific turning point where you felt, "Okay, the market finally gets what I'm doing"?

**VIVIENNE TAM:**  
Yes, definitely. I think the breakthrough came with my "MAO" collection in 1995, which I collaborated on with artist Zhang Hongtu. We took iconic images of Mao Zedong and rendered them in a humorous, pop-art style—Mao with pigtails, Mao in sunglasses. It created a huge sensation. It was bought by museums, worn by celebrities, and suddenly people realized that my work wasn't just about traditional aesthetics—it was about culture, commentary, and modern art.

**ANDREW STEVENS:**  
Let’s talk about the business side of that cultural shift. For decades, Western luxury brands looked at China primarily as a manufacturing hub, and later as a massive consumer market. But you’ve always pushed for "Designed in China" or "Created by Chinese talent." How have you seen that narrative evolve in the corporate boardroom?

**VIVIENNE TAM:**  
It has shifted dramatically. Twenty years ago, Chinese consumers wanted European labels—French, Italian, American. They looked outward for status. Today, especially with the younger generation, there is enormous pride in local culture and local design. We call it *Guochao*, or the "China-chic" trend. 

Now, international brands are trying to incorporate Chinese elements to appeal to this market, whereas before, I was one of the very few doing it globally. The boardroom perspective has changed from "How do we sell Western culture to China?" to "How do we respect and incorporate Chinese culture into a global brand?"

**ANDREW STEVENS:**  
You’ve expanded heavily across North America, Asia, and specifically Mainland China. From an operational standpoint, how do you balance managing a brand that operates across such culturally different markets?

**VIVIENNE TAM:**  
It requires flexibility. The core philosophy of the brand—harmony, culture, bridging worlds—remains the same everywhere. But the execution, the fit, the colors, and even the retail environment have to adapt. 

For instance, the retail space in China moves at lightning speed compared to New York or Europe. Digital integration, e-commerce, livestream shopping—these aren't just additions in China; they are the core of the business. You have to be agile. If you try to run an Asian fashion operation using a traditional 1990s Western retail model, you will fall behind very quickly.

**ANDREW STEVENS:**  
Speaking of innovation, you were one of the first fashion designers to cross over into technology—partnering with HP years ago to design a digital clutch laptop, and more recently dipping into tech-infused fashion and digital spaces. Why has tech been such a prominent part of your business strategy?

**VIVIENNE TAM:**  
Because fashion isn't just about clothes; it’s about lifestyle and communication. Technology is how we live today. When I designed the digital clutch with HP, people asked, "Why is a fashion designer doing tech?" But to me, a laptop or a smartphone is an accessory you carry every day—it should reflect your style just as much as your handbag. Integrating tech allows a brand to stay relevant to how people actually live their lives.

**ANDREW STEVENS:**  
Building a independent fashion brand and maintaining control over decades is famously difficult. The industry is dominated by massive luxury conglomerates. Have you ever been tempted to sell to a major group, or was staying independent crucial for you?

**VIVIENNE TAM:**  
There are always trade-offs. Being part of a big conglomerate gives you massive capital and global infrastructure. But independence gives you freedom—freedom of design, freedom of vision, and the ability to stay true to your identity without pressure for immediate, massive quarterly returns at the expense of brand integrity. I value my creative freedom immensely. 

**ANDREW STEVENS:**  
Looking forward, what do you see as the biggest challenge facing fashion leaders today? Is it sustainability, supply chain issues, or the fast-changing digital consumer?

**VIVIENNE TAM:**  
All of those, but sustainability is non-negotiable now. The industry produces too much waste. We have to look back at traditional principles—making things that last, using natural processes, respecting materials. Luxury in the future won't just be about the price tag; it will be about responsibility and story.

**ANDREW STEVENS:**  
Vivienne Tam, a fascinating journey and a wonderful vision for the future. Thank you so much for sharing your story with us on *The Boardroom*.

**VIVIENNE TAM:**  
Thank you, Andrew. It was my pleasure.

---

### **[SCENE END: STUDIO CUT]**

**ANDREW STEVENS (TO CAMERA):**  
From breaking down barriers in New York to pioneering modern cultural pride across Asia, Vivienne Tam has shown that staying true to one's roots isn't just good design—it’s smart business. 

That’s all for this edition of *The Boardroom*. I’m Andrew Stevens. Thank you for watching, and goodbye from Hong Kong.

### **[GRAPHIC: CNN CLOSING CREDITS / OUTRO MUSIC]**

**CNN Style** — 

# Balancing Art and Balance Sheets: Fashion Icon Elena Vance on Building a Global Empire

**By Sarah Lin, CNN**  
**Paris** — Published 8:00 AM EDT, Thursday, October 24, 2024

Sitting in her minimalist, light-drenched atelier overlooking the Seine, Elena Vance looks surprisingly relaxed for someone who just wrapped up a 72-look Paris Fashion Week showcase. 

Outside, the fashion world is still buzzing over her latest Spring/Summer collection—a masterclass in architectural tailoring and fluid silks. But inside the headquarters of *VANCE*, the luxury fashion house she founded two decades ago, the focus has already shifted. 

"The runway show is thirty minutes of magic," Vance tells CNN, taking a sip of black espresso. "The other 364 days of the year are about logistics, margins, supply chains, and keeping a three-billion-dollar machine turning without losing its soul."

Vance belongs to a rare tier of fashion icons. In an industry where creative directors are often shuffled like deck chairs and CEOs rarely touch a sketchpad, she remains both the Creative Director and Chief Executive Officer of her brand. Under her dual leadership, *VANCE* has expanded into 42 countries, entering cosmetics, eyewear, and high jewelry while maintaining an enviable 20% year-over-year growth.

CNN sat down with Vance to discuss the delicate dance between raw creativity and corporate strategy, navigating a shifting global luxury market, and how she keeps the spark alive amid the noise of a global brand.

***

### The Art of Commerce

**CNN:** You’ve built one of the few truly independent luxury conglomerates left in fashion. Many designers detest the business side of the industry. How do you reconcile the artist with the CEO?

**Elena Vance:** I learned early on that business acumen isn't the enemy of creativity—it’s its ultimate protector. If you don't understand your balance sheet, someone else will, and then they will tell you what you can and cannot create. 

A dress can be a masterpiece, but if it doesn't sell, it’s just a sculpture sitting in a warehouse. I don't look at commerce as a compromise; I look at it as communication. The market telling you 'we love this' or 'this didn't resonate' is data. I use that data to fuel my next creative impulse, not to constrain it.

**CNN:** How do you structure your mind—and your calendar—to switch between designing a collection and reviewing quarterly earnings?

**Vance:** Compartmentalization and discipline. Mondays and Wednesdays are 'spreadsheet days'—board meetings, supply chain reviews, retail expansion strategies in Asia and North America. Tuesdays and Thursdays are for the studio—draping, color theory, casting. 

Fridays are mixed. But the rule is: when I am in the atelier, the door is closed to financial crisis unless the building is literally burning. If you let corporate anxiety bleed into the creative process, the clothes lose their romance. And in luxury, romance is your primary asset.

### Navigating a Changing Global Landscape

**CNN:** The luxury market is facing headwinds, particularly with shifting consumer habits in China and rising inflation globally. How is *VANCE* adapting without diluting its high-end appeal?

**Vance:** The definition of luxury has changed. It used to be about exclusivity and status. Today, especially for younger demographics, it’s about authenticity, provenance, and emotional connection. 

When economic times get tough, consumers perform a 'quality flight.' They stop buying mid-tier, disposable trends and invest in pieces that hold value—both financial and emotional. So, our strategy isn't to discount or chase viral, cheap trends. It’s to double down on extreme craftsmanship. We’re opening smaller, highly bespoke flagships rather than massive, sterile department store counters. You have to respect the nuance of every market. What works in London does not work in Chengdu.

**CNN:** Speaking of viral trends, social media moves at a breakneck pace. How do you balance the pressure for constant 'content' with the slower pace of true design?

**Vance:** You have to know who you are. If you chase every TikTok algorithm, you become noise. We embrace digital technology—our supply chain uses AI for demand forecasting to reduce fabric waste by 30%, which is massive for sustainability. But creatively? I refuse to design for a five-second scroll. The garment has to feel extraordinary when you touch it in real life. That is a boundary I will not cross.

### The Legacy of Leadership

**CNN:** You have thousands of employees globally. What has being a leader taught you about creativity?

**Vance:** That my job is no longer just to be creative, but to cultivate an environment where *other* people can be creative and courageous. When you start out, you think leadership is about control. As you grow a global brand, you realize leadership is about surrender. You hire brilliant people—whether they are master tailors or brilliant CFOs—and you give them the vision, then get out of their way.

**CNN:** Looking ahead to the next twenty years of the brand, what keeps you motivated?

**Vance:** The blank page. Every season, no matter how big the business gets, it still comes down to a blank piece of paper, a pencil, and an idea. As long as that terrifies and excites me in equal measure, I’ll keep doing both jobs.

She used to make all the clothes for our family—for me, my brothers, my sisters, and herself. I used to sit beside her for hours, watching her transform a simple piece of fabric into something beautiful and functional. 

**ANDREW STEVENS:** Did she teach you how to sew?

**VIVIENNE TAM:** She taught me how to sew, but more importantly, she taught me resourcefulness. **CNN Style** — 

# How Vivienne Tam built a global fashion empire by bridging East and West

**By** CNN Style Staff  
**Published** 8:00 AM EDT, Mon October 23, 2023

---

**(CNN) —** Long before "fusion" became a buzzword in global luxury, Vivienne Tam was quietly revolutionary. Born in Guangzhou, China, and raised in Hong Kong, the designer moved to New York City in the late 1980s with little more than a bag of her own creations and an unyielding vision: to introduce authentic Chinese culture to contemporary Western fashion.

Decades later, Tam is widely credited with pioneering "China Chic." Her high-profile designs—including her iconic 1995 "Mao" pop-art collection—are held in the permanent archives of prestigious institutions like the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Victoria and Albert Museum. Today, her namesake brand boasts more than 30 boutique stores worldwide, alongside major retail presence across Asia and the Americas, and early collaborations with tech giants like Hewlett-Packard.

Sitting down with CNN at her light-filled Manhattan atelier, Tam reflected on her journey from a modest Hong Kong upbringing to managing a global retail footprint, her history of breaking boundaries, and why cultural heritage remains her greatest source of inspiration.

*This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.*

---

### **Finding the Thread: Early Beginnings**

**CNN:** You’ve often spoken about growing up in Hong Kong and the deep influence your family had on your aesthetic. Where did your love for fashion truly begin?

**Vivienne Tam:** It really started with my mother. Growing up, money was tight, so my mother made clothes for us. I used to sit beside her, watching her take a simple piece of fabric, fold it, cut it, and turn it into something beautiful that we could wear. It felt like magic to me. 

By the age of eight, I was already redesigning my own clothes and making outfits for my siblings. I realized very early that clothing wasn't just utility—it was identity, emotion, and self-expression.

**CNN:** You later studied at Hong Kong Polytechnic University. What was the fashion landscape like there at the time?

**Tam:** Back then, Hong Kong was primarily a manufacturing hub for Western brands. People looked to Paris, London, and New York for inspiration. No one was really looking inward at Chinese heritage as a source of high fashion. 

When I graduated, I knew I wanted to create something of my own, but I also realized that to make a global impact, I had to step outside of my comfort zone. That’s what brought me to New York.

---

### **Taking Manhattan: The Early New York Days**

**CNN:** Moving to New York in the late 1980s was a bold step. What was it like trying to make a mark in one of the toughest fashion capitals in the world?

**Tam:** It was terrifying and exhilarating all at once. I remember walking up and down Seventh Avenue carrying a giant tote bag filled with my sample dresses, knocking on doors of buyers at department stores. 

Many people didn't understand what I was doing. They would look at my designs—which incorporated traditional Chinese embroidery, mandarin collars, and dragon motifs—and say, "This looks like a souvenir." But I refused to alter my vision to fit European-centric ideas of fashion. I knew there was a modern way to translate East Asian culture for the modern, global woman.

---

```
"I walked up Seventh Avenue carrying a giant tote bag filled with my samples... Many people didn't understand. They said, 'This looks like a souvenir.' But I refused to alter my vision."
— Vivienne Tam
```

---

**CNN:** Your breakthrough came in the mid-1990s, particularly with your 1995 "Mao" collection, created in collaboration with artist Zhang Hongtu. Did you anticipate the global reaction to that collection?

**Tam:** Not at all! I just wanted to take iconic imagery that had caused so much pain historically and neutralize it through art, humor, and pop art—putting pigtails or a nose ring on Chairman Mao. 

It was controversial, yes. Some stores refused to display it in their windows, but artists and curators loved it. When the Metropolitan Museum of Art acquired pieces from that collection, it was a turning point. It proved that Asian-inspired design wasn't just a fleeting trend; it was a legitimate, powerful artistic movement.

---

### **Building a Global Footprint: Expanding to 30+ Stores**

**CNN:** Today, you have over 30 stores worldwide, with a massive presence across Tokyo, Hong Kong, Beijing, and North America. How did you transition from a independent designer in New York to managing a retail empire?

**Tam:** Growth has to be organic and rooted in understanding your customer. Our first major retail expansion outside the U.S. started in Asia, particularly Japan and Hong Kong. There was a hunger among modern Asian women to see their own culture elevated into high-end, contemporary fashion.

Opening stores isn't just about selling clothes; it's about creating a universe. Each of our 30 stores is designed to feel like an extension of the brand's philosophy—a harmony of Feng Shui principles, modern architecture, and traditional craftsmanship. Managing that scale requires incredible discipline, a strong team, and listening closely to local markets while keeping the core identity consistent.

**CNN:** You were also one of the first fashion designers to embrace technology—working with HP in 2008 to design the "digital clutch" laptop, long before fashion-tech was popular. What drove that forward-thinking strategy?

**Tam:** I’ve always viewed technology as another fabric. Why shouldn't our digital devices be as stylish as our handbags? When HP approached me, tech products were mostly black, heavy boxes. I wanted to make something feminine, elegant, and functional. 

To me, bridging East and West also means bridging tradition and innovation. Today, that means exploring Web3, digital fashion, and sustainable textiles. Fashion cannot stand still.

---

### **Legacy and the Future**

**CNN:** Looking back at your career—from a young girl in Hong Kong watching her mother sew, to a global icon with dozens of stores—what is the biggest lesson you’ve learned about staying relevant in fashion for over three decades?

**Tam:** Authenticity. Trends come and go at an incredible speed, especially today with social media. If you try to chase every trend, you lose your soul. 

Throughout my career, whether I’m designing a gown, opening a new boutique in Shanghai, or experimenting with digital art, my core anchor has stayed the same: celebrating culture, bringing people together, and creating harmony. If you stay true to your narrative, the world will eventually tune in.

**CNN:** What’s next for the Vivienne Tam brand?

**Tam:** We are continuing to expand our physical footprint, particularly looking at new markets in the Middle East and Southeast Asia, while expanding our lifestyle and wellness lines. But most importantly, I want to keep mentoring young Asian designers. When I started, there were very few doors open for us. My goal now is to leave those doors wide open for the next generation.
